notes.meaning: Job feels completely exhausted by his suffering and says he hates his own life. He decides to hold nothing back and speak out all the bitter sorrow in his soul. He feels he has reached the point where he has nothing left to lose by being totally honest with God.

Job begs God not to treat him like a guilty criminal. He asks God to reveal the specific charges against him so he can understand why this trial is happening. When we face deep trouble, it is natural to ask God to show us what He is teaching us.

Job asks if it truly brings God pleasure to crush someone He created. It seems to Job that God is throwing away His own handiwork while letting wicked people flourish in their schemes. In his confusion, Job struggles to understand why a good God would allow the innocent to suffer while evil people prosper.

Job asks whether God sees with limited human eyes. Human beings have weak eyesight, cannot see into darkness, and judge only by outward appearances. God, however, knows all hidden truths and sees right into the human heart.

Job asks whether God's life is brief and fleeting like that of a mortal man. A human judge has only a short time on earth and must rush to investigate a suspect before dying. God lives forever, so He has no need to hurry or press someone to uncover secret facts.

Job asks why God seems to search so eagerly for some hidden flaw in his life. God already knows Job is not an ungodly hypocrite, and Job has nowhere to flee from God's sovereign power. Because Job cannot escape God's hand anyway, he wonders why God treats him with such harsh pressure.

Job points out that God's own hands skillfully shaped every part of his body. It bewilders him that the loving Creator who took such care to form him would now turn around to tear him down. He appeals to God's tender care as the master craftsman of human life.

Job asks God to remember that He formed him out of soft clay, just as a potter molds a vessel. A potter usually values the work He spent time making rather than smashing it to pieces. Job wonders why God would take a fragile human vessel and turn him back into dust so quickly.

Job uses the image of cheese-making to describe the mystery of how a baby forms in the womb. Just as liquid milk is poured out and curdles into a solid shape, an unborn child grows and firms up by God's power. Job sees God's active hand at work in the very beginning of human life.

Job explains how God clothed him with skin and flesh and held his body together with bones and sinews. God acted like a master weaver, knitting every joint and muscle into place. Every human life is carefully put together by God's creative design.

Job acknowledges that God gave him the gift of physical life and watched over him with faithful love. God's daily providence and tender care kept him breathing and safe through all his earlier years. Even in intense pain, Job does not forget that God has shown him great goodness in the past.

Job suspects that God had planned this sudden misery all along, keeping it hidden in His heart. He fears that even while God was blessing him, God intended to bring these crushing troubles in the end. Job cannot yet understand the loving purposes God worked out behind the scenes.

Job feels as though God is watching him with strict legal judgment. He worries that if he slips up in the least, God will immediately mark it down and refuse to show him mercy. In his deep distress, Job feels closely guarded and condemned rather than forgiven.

Job feels completely trapped whether he does evil or good. If he were wicked, he would face ruin; yet even as an upright man, he is too overwhelmed by shame and pain to lift his head. In his utter confusion, he asks God to look upon his misery and take pity on him.

Job feels that if he dares to lift his head or defend himself, God hunts him down like a ferocious lion. Instead of ending his life quickly, God seems to return again and again with astonishing power against him. Job feels helpless before God's overwhelming strength.

Job compares his mounting afflictions to a line of courtroom witnesses proving his supposed guilt. Each fresh wave of illness and grief feels like a new battalion in an army attacking him without rest. He feels completely worn down by unending waves of trouble.

Job asks why God ever allowed him to survive birth if his life was destined for such agony. He wishes he had died at delivery so that no eye would ever have seen his pain. In his deepest depression, Job feels that being carried straight from the womb to the grave would have been better than this terrible suffering.

Job points out that he has only a few short days left to live. He begs God to pull back His heavy hand and give him just a brief moment of relief before he dies. Even a small taste of comfort would bring rest to someone in constant pain.

Job looks ahead to death as a journey to a shadowy realm from which no one returns. Before Christ brought the full light of eternal life, the grave seemed to ancient believers like a gloomy place of total disorder, where even the light was like black midnight. Job simply longs for a quiet moment of relief before stepping into that great darkness.
